title: Christ is alive (Christus Vivit 1)
hook: Francis's letter to young people opens: Christ is alive and wants you alive
tomorrow: why name a letter about love in the past tense?

segments.voice: Last week closed at a market stall, with a woman who wouldn't join the gossip. Holiness, Francis said, grows through small gestures.

The bus ride home after a loss is quiet in a heavy way. Hoods up. Earbuds in. Somebody's leg bouncing. Everyone a little older than they were at kickoff. Now open a letter written for exactly those people. No greeting. No "dear young friends." Just an exclamation, the first words on the page: Christ is alive! It's called Christus Vivit, and Pope Francis wrote it to young people after a synod of bishops met to listen to them. The next line is the one he says he wants every young Christian to hear first.
screen: `THE QUIET BUS RIDE HOME.` → `NO GREETING.` → `CHRIST IS ALIVE!`

segments.voice: Here it is: Christ is alive, and he wants you to be alive. Francis doesn't leave it as a doctrine on a page. Christ is our hope, he says, and he brings youth to the world: everything he touches becomes young, new, full of life. Then it gets personal. He is in you, he is with you, and he never abandons you. However far you wander, the Risen One is there, calling you and waiting for you to come back and start over. And when you feel yourself growing old, from sorrow, resentment or fear, from doubt or failure, he'll be there to restore your strength and your hope. So what does young mean here? Not a number of birthdays. In Francis's picture, sorrow and resentment can age anyone, on a bus or in a hospital bed, and contact with Christ makes things young again. He adds that while he writes to young people, he's speaking to the whole people of God as well. So the opening is Easter in the present tense. Not he lived. He is alive.
screen: `HE WANTS YOU ALIVE.` · `EVERYTHING HE TOUCHES BECOMES YOUNG.` · `SORROW CAN AGE ANYONE.` · `COME BACK AND START OVER.` · then, large: `HE IS ALIVE.`

segments.voice: If you can, get up and walk for a minute, around the room or out the door, at an easy pace. Let each few steps carry the line in the present tense, Christ is alive, and notice your own breath and legs, alive too. If you pray, tell him one place you'd like to start over.
Christ is alive. The first words of Francis's letter to young people: he is alive, and he wants you alive.
Carry this: he is alive, present tense, on an ordinary Tuesday or the bus ride home. Off you go.

howItsDone: Young Catholics and their parishes read Christus Vivit in youth groups and at gatherings, often starting from its opening cry, Christ is alive.

fork.setup: your uncle, sixty and newly retired, says he feels useless and old. what does Christus Vivit's opening offer him?
options: that letter is for young people, so nothing.
feeling old comes from sorrow and fear, and Christ waits for anyone to start over.

fork.reveal: Francis says sorrow, fear and failure make people feel old, the Risen One waits for them to come back and start over, and the letter speaks to the whole people of God.

chat.says: lost tonight. whole team's flat, me too. i feel about 80. ok but how does 'he's alive' help?
options: Francis says sorrow makes anyone feel old, and Christ waits for you to start over. Practice is a restart.
It helps once you feel happy again. Francis says young means having no sorrow at all.
It doesn't, really. 'He's alive' is about Easter Sunday, not a bad night after a game.
chat.meaning: In Christus Vivit, sorrow, fear and failure can make anyone feel old; the Risen One is there to restore strength and help you start over.
